sentences.text: Ernesto taught her how the camera worked.
He showed her the aperture ring, and the focus ring, and the small window at the top that told you how many pictures were left on the roll.
He explained that the camera did not need batteries — that everything about it was mechanical, and would work anywhere in the world, at any temperature, if you kept it dry.
He showed her how to advance the film, and how to press the shutter release with the pad of her finger and not the tip, so the camera did not jerk.
She learned it quickly.
She was patient in the way that ten-year-olds can be when they are being taken seriously.
The first afternoon she used the whole first roll — thirty-six exposures — in about two hours.
She took pictures of the water, and of the horizon, and of the mountains floating, and of her father's boots reflected upside-down.
Ernesto did not tell her to be careful about the film.
He said, "Use it.
That is what it is for.
I have two more rolls in the jeep."
That evening they stayed at a small lodge at the edge of the Salar — a low building whose walls were made of blocks of salt cut from the Salar itself.
Even the tables inside were made of salt.
It was warm and dim and smelled faintly of salt and woodsmoke.
There were maybe eight other guests — a few Bolivian families like themselves, a small group of Japanese tourists, one older German couple.
And in the corner, at a small table by the woodstove, sat an old man with a white beard and a very worn dark green field jacket.
He was drinking coffee and reading a book.
Ernesto looked over and grinned.
He said, "Elena.
Come.
That is Don Juan." And he took her to the corner.
Don Juan was seventy years old, and had been a landscape photographer his entire adult life, and had come to the Salar every February for the past forty years to photograph it.
Ernesto knew him — everyone in the small Bolivian scientific community knew Don Juan — and greeted him warmly.
Don Juan smiled up at Elena and shook her hand seriously, as if she were an adult, which pleased her.
"Show her," Ernesto said.
Don Juan opened the folder on the table.
Inside were maybe forty large black-and-white photographs, all taken at the Salar.
Some showed the mirror.
Some showed the dry season, the white cracked hexagons.
Some showed people, small, walking.
Some showed just the sky.
Elena looked at them one by one.
They were the most beautiful photographs she had ever seen.
She could not stop looking.
After she had looked at all of them, Elena asked, "Don Juan, why do you keep taking pictures of the same place?
Forty years is a long time." Don Juan smiled.
He said, "Because it is not the same place, hija.
It looks the same to a person passing through once.
But it is different every day.
Every hour.
The light changes.
The wind changes.
The water changes with the seasons and the rain.
When there is no wind, it is a mirror.
When there is a breeze, the mirror breaks into a million small facets.
When there are clouds, the whole Salar is dark.
When there are no clouds, the whole Salar is like a page.
And I am different every day too.
What I notice today is not what I noticed yesterday.
So I keep coming.
And I keep taking pictures.
And they keep being different pictures.
It does not end."
Elena thought about that.
She looked at her father.
Her father was watching her, quiet, half-smiling.
Later, walking back to their room in the salt-brick lodge, she said, "Papi, do you know why you never took pictures?" Ernesto was quiet for many steps.
Then he said, "I have wondered this for thirty years.
I think I know now.
Do you want the answer?" Elena nodded.
In their small warm room, wrapped in heavy woolen blankets against the cold Andean night, Ernesto sat on the edge of his bed and told her.
He said, "When I was young, I noticed that if I took a picture of something — really tried to compose the picture — I stopped seeing what was in front of me.
I went to the other side of the camera.
I was making a picture instead of being there.
I could not do both.
Some people can do both.
Don Juan can do both.
It is a gift.
I did not have that gift.
So I chose.
I chose to see.
And I stopped taking pictures.
I carried the camera anyway, all these years, because my father gave it to me.
And I never quite wanted to admit to myself that I was choosing not to use it.
So it was easier to carry it, empty, and pretend I might use it someday."
Elena said, "So why did you put a film in it now?" Ernesto smiled at her.
He said, "Because now there is someone I want to take pictures.
Not me.
You.
When you look at something, mi hija, I see it new.
That is what watching a child watch the world does for a parent.
It gives them the world back.
If you take pictures this week, I get to see you seeing.
That is a different thing than seeing the Salar.
That is what I want.
Watching someone see is a way of loving them.
I did not know that when I was twenty.
I know it now." He was quiet for a moment.
"So — you take the pictures.
I will watch you."
